title: Cranial Nerves IX and X (The Glossopharyngeal and Vagus Nerves)
subtitle: Localize palate, pharynx and larynx deficits from supranuclear to nuclear, jugular foramen and laryngeal nerve lesions

points.text: IX, X and XI leave the medulla together and share the jugular foramen, so lesions there rarely spare a single nerve.
points.quote: These three nerves then travel together through the jugular foramen.

points.text: IX motor fibers come from the rostral nucleus ambiguus and supply the stylopharyngeus.
points.quote: The motor fibers originate from the rostral nucleus ambiguus and innervate the stylopharyngeus muscle (a pharyngeal elevator)

points.text: IX carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue.
points.quote: The sensory fibers carried in the glossopharyngeal nerve include taste afferents, supplying the posterior third of the tongue and the pharynx

points.text: Parasympathetic IX fibers start in the inferior salivatory nucleus and end in the parotid gland, via the otic ganglion.
points.quote: The parasympathetic fibers carried in the glossopharyngeal nerve originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus, located in the periventricular gray matter of the rostral medulla

points.text: Taste over the posterior third of the tongue can be tested and is lost on the side of a nerve lesion.
points.quote: The integrity of taste sensation may be tested over the posterior third of the tongue and is lost ipsilaterally with nerve lesions.

points.text: Vagal motor fibers arise from two nuclei: the dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic) and the nucleus ambiguus (striated muscle).
points.quote: The motor fibers carried in the vagus nerve arise from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and the nucleus ambiguus.

points.text: The nucleus ambiguus supplies the striated muscles of palate, pharynx and larynx, with the exceptions of tensor veli palatini and stylopharyngeus.
points.quote: Fibers from this nucleus supply all of the striated musculature of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx except the tensor veli palatini (cranial nerve V)

points.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, which belongs to the superior laryngeal nerve.
points.quote: The recurrent laryngeal nerves then divide into anterior and posterior rami, which supply all of the muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid muscle

points.text: The vagus carries sensation from the concha of the ear (auricular branch) to the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
points.quote: Exteroceptive sensation from the concha of the ear is carried by the vagus (jugular ganglion) to terminate in the descending (spinal) nucleus

points.text: The afferent limb of the gag reflex is IX; the efferent limb uses both IX and X.
points.quote: The afferent limb of the pharyngeal reflex (gag reflex) runs in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the efferent limb runs in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

localizationRules.explanation: Expect combined IX and X findings; look at neighbouring structures to place the lesion.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions affecting the glossopharyngeal nerve also usually involve the vagus, and syndromes affecting both nerves are therefore much more common

localizationRules.explanation: A single cortical or corticobulbar lesion does not produce a deficit because the nucleus ambiguus has bilateral input.
localizationRules.quote: Supranuclear lesions, if unilateral, do not result in any neurologic deficit because of bilateral corticobulbar input to the nucleus ambiguus.

localizationRules.explanation: These involve neighbouring cranial nerves and brainstem structures, so localize by the accompanying signs (for example Wallenberg syndrome).
localizationRules.quote: Such lesions commonly involve other cranial nerves, especially the vagus, and other brainstem structures (e.g., Wallenberg syndrome)

localizationRules.explanation: On phonation the weak side fails to rise and the uvula is pulled toward the normal side.
localizationRules.quote: with phonation, the ipsilateral palate fails to elevate, and the uvula is retracted toward the nonparalyzed side

localizationRules.rule: Gag reflex in a vagal lesion
localizationRules.explanation: A unilateral vagal lesion depresses the gag reflex on its own side because it breaks the efferent limb.
localizationRules.quote: Therefore, unilateral vagal lesions depress the ipsilateral gag reflex by interrupting the efferent arc.

keySyndromes.name: Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral trapezius and sternocleidomastoid paresis and atrophy (XI) + Dysphonia, dysphagia, depressed gag reflex, palatal droop and homolateral vocal cord paralysis (IX, X) + Loss of taste and anesthesia of the posterior third of the tongue, soft palate, pharynx and larynx + Often dull aching pain behind the ear
keySyndromes.clue: IX, X and XI together; the hypoglossal nerve is spared (compare Collet-Sicard).
keySyndromes.quote: Lesions at the jugular foramen, especially glomus jugulare tumors and basal skull fractures, injure cranial nerves IX, X, and XI

keySyndromes.name: Collet-Sicard syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Palsy of cranial nerves IX + X + XI + XII
keySyndromes.clue: Seen with retropharyngeal or retroparotid space lesions; Villaret syndrome adds the sympathetic chain and occasionally cranial nerve VII.
keySyndromes.quote: Resulting syndromes include the Collet-Sicard syndrome (affecting cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII)

keySyndromes.name: Avellis syndrome (palatopharyngeal paralysis)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral palatal paralysis + Ipsilateral pharyngeal paralysis + Laryngeal function spared
keySyndromes.clue: A lesion confined to the more cephalad nucleus ambiguus, owing to its somatotopic organization.
keySyndromes.quote: When only the more cephalad portion of the nucleus ambiguus is injured, laryngeal function is spared (palatopharyngeal paralysis of Avellis)

keySyndromes.name: Glossopharyngeal (vagoglossopharyngeal) neuralgia
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral stabbing paroxysmal pain in throat or ear + Lasting seconds to minutes + Triggered by chewing, coughing, talking, yawning or swallowing
keySyndromes.clue: No neurologic deficit in the primary form; attacks may bring syncope through reflex bradycardia and asystole.
keySyndromes.quote: refers to a unilateral pain (usually stabbing, sharp, and paroxysmal) located in the field of sensory distribution of the glossopharyngeal or vagus nerves

keySyndromes.name: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
keySyndromes.triad: Hoarseness, often transient + Flaccid dysphonia with breathiness and mild inhalatory stridor + Paralyzed vocal cord near the midline + Palatopharyngeal function normal
keySyndromes.clue: Cricothyroid is spared because the superior laryngeal nerve supplies it; the left nerve is injured more often.
keySyndromes.quote: With unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, unilateral paralysis of all laryngeal muscles (except the cricothyroid, which is innervated by the superior laryngeal nerve) occurs.

keySyndromes.name: Syncope from glossopharyngeal or vagal metastasis
keySyndromes.triad: Severe paroxysms of pain in neck, ear or side of head + Syncope from sudden hypotension + Sometimes bradycardia
keySyndromes.clue: Typically in head and neck cancer, especially when the tumor recurs after treatment; may be the only symptom.
keySyndromes.quote: Syncope with or without pain may be the only symptom of metastatic involvement of the glossopharyngeal or vagus nerve

boardTraps.text: In pseudobulbar states the gag reflex can be depressed or exaggerated, so its presence does not exclude bilateral corticobulbar disease.
boardTraps.quote: With stimulation, the gag reflex may be depressed or markedly exaggerated, resulting in severe retching and even vomiting.

boardTraps.text: An isolated IX lesion is subtle: motor weakness may be negligible, with at most mild dysphagia.
boardTraps.quote: Motor paresis may be negligible with glossopharyngeal nerve lesions, although mild dysphagia may occur

boardTraps.text: A superior laryngeal nerve lesion causes few findings because the nerve is mainly sensory; the cricothyroid is the only motor target.
boardTraps.quote: Lesions of this nerve result in few clinical findings because this branch is primarily sensory.

boardTraps.text: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer and is injured more often than the right.
boardTraps.quote: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right and is therefore damaged more often.

boardTraps.text: A unilateral vagal lesion leaves the vocal cord in the cadaveric position and, despite impaired voluntary cough, causes little dyspnea.
boardTraps.quote: The ipsilateral vocal cord assumes the cadaveric position (midway between adduction and abduction), and although voluntary coughing may be impaired, there is little dyspnea.

boardTraps.text: Unlike trigeminal neuralgia, glossopharyngeal neuralgia is very rarely caused by multiple sclerosis.
boardTraps.quote: Multiple sclerosis is an extremely rare etiology for this syndrome
